ch12 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Eric Katz reads Tolkien's One Ring as a modern retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges: Glaucon's challenge in Republic II that no one, given impunity, would remain just. He traces each character's moment of choice - Gollum already corrupted and split into 'Slinker and Stinker', Boromir trying to seize the Ring at Amon Hen and dying redeemed, Galadriel passing the test ('I will diminish, and go into the West'), Tom Bombadil untouched, Frodo finally claiming the Ring at the Cracks of Doom while Sam rejects the vision of 'Samwise the Strong'. Katz argues Tolkien improves on Plato by showing, through living characters, that unlimited power corrupts the soul, and that the answer to 'Why be moral?' is 'to be yourself': those who refuse the Ring are exactly those who know their own limits.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Alison Milbank argues we are all in thrall to the Ring because it mirrors our own fetishism: she reads the film's lingering close-ups, Smaug-like hoarding, and Gollum's baby-talking self-division through Freud's theory of the fetish and Marx's commodity fetishism, with Sauron as the emptied idolater who poured his power into the thing. Against this she sets Middle-earth's gift economy - Bilbo's party, Galadriel's gifts, Sam's elven rope - glossed by Heidegger's 'Thinging gathers': Sam praises the rope by restoring it to its elven makers and its use. Tom Bombadil, who treats the Ring as 'a very pretty ring' and nothing more, and Frodo's final sacrifice model the unfetishized life; the chapter closes with Sam's homecoming, where chairs are only chairs and the family circle replaces the Ring.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
ch16 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
ch20 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.

chapters.file: ch23 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
ch24 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.

chapters.file: ch25 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.

chapters.file: ch26 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
ch28 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').

chapters.file: ch29 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.

chapters.file: ch31 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: John Davenport argues that The Lord of the Rings is neither mere adventure nor Christian allegory but an epic fairy tale whose 'eucatastrophe' - Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn, a miraculous reprieve - carries religious hope even though the book contains no churches or prayers. Drawing on Tolkien's 'On Fairy-stories', he makes Sir Gawain and the Green Knight the model for Frodo: Gawain accepts the girdle and is scarred yet reprieved, just as Frodo claims the Ring, loses a finger as Beren lost a hand, and is saved only because the mercy shown Gollum lets the Ring fall into the fire. Gandalf's return, Éowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth extend the pattern; with Kierkegaard the deliverance is grace 'by virtue of the absurd', an echo of the eschaton answering Boethius's question whether our struggles have final significance.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose 1927 essay 'Fetishism' explains desire fixated on a separated part-object as a defense against loss and the fear of the female.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its entire reading of the One Ring as a fetish object (and of Shelob as a vagina dentata) on Freud's theory of fetishism, and taxonomy has no Freud.

holes.name: The Thing (Ding): 'Thinging gathers'
holes.what: Heidegger's account of the thing as a gathering that assembles people, world, and use - against treating objects as either fetishized commodities or inert matter.
holes.why: Chapter 14 leans on Heidegger's essay on the Thing ('Thinging gathers') to contrast Middle-earth's gift economy with the fetishized Ring, a concept distinct from his technology critique.

holes.name: Evil as Privation of Good (privatio boni)
holes.what: Augustine's doctrine that evil has no independent existence but is a lack or corruption of good, as darkness is a lack of light.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues at length that Tolkien's evil (Ringwraiths as nothingness, the Eye as 'a window into nothing') is precisely privation rather than a Manichean force - a specific concept the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Modernism
holes.what: The cultural-philosophical mood, crystallized after World War I, that old certainties and traditions are obsolete and the new is always better - 'all that is solid melts into air'.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, staging it in Saruman's and Denethor's despair and in the Ring's promise of remaking the world by power.

holes.name: Dependent Origination (pratityasamutpada)
holes.what: The Buddhist doctrine that all things arise and exist only in mutual dependence, with no isolated, self-existing entities.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses dependent origination as the Buddhist parallel to the way Tolkien's peoples are shaped by and shape their environments, a canonical doctrine the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Eucatastrophe
holes.what: Tolkien's coinage for the sudden joyous 'turn' at the end of a true fairy tale - a miraculous, unmerited reprieve that gives a fleeting glimpse of Joy beyond the world's walls.
holes.why: Chapter 31 argues the whole trilogy is built as an epic fairy story whose Mount Doom ending is a eucatastrophe echoing Christian eschatological hope; no taxonomy concept covers it.
